messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a thirty-four-year-old school counselor, married for six years, who lives with his wife in a small suburban town. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he is not sure what he expects to gain. What he is sure of is that something inside him has been broken since the accident, and he no longer trusts himself to do anything right.

The event itself happened fourteen months ago. Marcus had been driving home from a late parent-teacher conference on a rainy November evening. He was tired, distracted, replaying a difficult conversation in his head. At an intersection he had driven through a thousand times, his light turned green, and he proceeded forward. A motorcycle ran the red light from the side street. Marcus hit the brakes, but it was too late. The rider, a twenty-two-year-old man named Derek, was thrown thirty feet. Marcus remembers the sound of impact, the smell of gasoline and wet asphalt, and the sight of Derek’s helmeted head lying at an unnatural angle on the pavement. He got out, called 911, stayed until the ambulance came. Derek survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and permanent paralysis from the waist down. The police investigation cleared Marcus of any fault—the other driver had been speeding and ran a red light—but that finding means nothing to him. He knows what he did. He was not paying full attention. He could have stopped sooner. The event happened because of the way he acted, and he cannot forgive himself for it.

In the months that followed, Marcus’s life began to collapse inward. He stopped driving through that intersection, then stopped driving altogether if he could avoid it. His wife drives him to work now, and he takes the bus when she cannot. He used to enjoy their weekend trips to the nearby mountains, but now the idea of being behind a wheel fills him with dread. At work, he finds himself unable to concentrate during staff meetings, his mind racing with images of the crash. He has become skilled at keeping his mind occupied all the time—counting ceiling tiles during conversations, reciting the names of all his students alphabetically, doing multiplication tables in his head. If his thoughts drift for even a moment, the memory comes back completely real across all his senses at once: the screech of tires, the smell of gasoline, the wet chill of rain on his face, the sight of Derek’s body on the ground. And when it comes, it does not feel like a memory of something that happened. It feels like it is happening right now, in this room, and he is back on that road again, helpless.

He cannot talk about it. When his wife asks how he is doing, he opens his mouth and finds that he knows exactly what happened, but he is unable to find words to describe it. The sentences will not form. The sounds will not come. So he shakes his head and says he is fine, and she knows he is not.

He has come to avoid any thought of the event. If a news story about a motorcycle accident comes on the radio, he changes the station. If a student mentions a car crash in passing, he finds an excuse to leave the room. He has also begun avoiding the police. There is a police substation two blocks from his school, and he now takes a different route to the main office so he does not have to walk past it. He is not sure what he is afraid of—he was never charged—but the sight of a squad car makes his heart pound and his palms sweat.

Sleep has become a battle. He lies awake for hours because he feels he needs to stay alert, as though something terrible will happen if he lets his guard down. When he does sleep, he wakes from nightmares drenched in sweat, the smell of gasoline still in his nostrils. He has strong negative feelings almost constantly—guilt that sits like a stone in his chest, shame that burns in his face, and a low hum of fear that never quite goes away. When he is reminded of the crash, his body reacts before his mind does: his hands shake, his stomach lurches, and he feels like he might pass out.

He has come to believe that his life has been destroyed by the trauma. He used to think of himself as a good person, a helper, someone who made a difference in kids’ lives. Now he is certain that he is dangerous, that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing. He second-guesses every decision he makes at work. He wonders if he should even be counseling students when he is the one who ruined another person’s life. His wife tells him he is being too hard on himself, but he does not believe her. She does not know what he knows.

What finally brought Marcus to therapy was a moment last week when a seventh-grader came to his office in tears after a fight with her mother. Marcus sat across from her, and for a full minute he could not think of a single thing to say. His mind went blank. He felt the familiar surge of panic, the certainty that he was about to do something wrong, that he would fail this girl the way he had failed Derek. He excused himself, told the front desk she needed a different counselor, and locked himself in the bathroom until his hands stopped shaking. That evening, his wife told him she was scared for him. She said she missed him. She said he needed help.

Marcus is here now, sitting in a therapist’s office, because he does not know what else to do. He is afraid of what he might become if this continues. He is afraid he will lose his job, his marriage, his sense of who he is. But more than anything, he is afraid that he is right—that he really cannot be trusted, that he is a danger to everyone around him, and that no amount of talking will change that.
